Freeze casting or ice templating of materials for making porous microstructures without the addition of thermally fugitive pore formers provides a columnar pore morphology through the thickness of the membrane with exceptionally low tortuosity that has applications in catalyst supports, electrochemical cells, filtration/transport media, composite fabrication and biomaterials (Liu, R. et al., 2016 & Liu W. L. et al., 2012). Figure 1. Freeze tape casting process of fabricating low tortuosity, graded pores through the tape thickness (left) in which pores are uniquely aligned long range through the length of the tape (top). Representative micrographs depict graded pore geometry as the dark regions (right) (bar = 100 microns) Hybridization of freeze casting with commercially scalable tape casting methods (Figure 1), pioneered at MSU (Sofie, S. W. et al., 2007 & Driscoll, D. et al., 2011), provides scalable and long-range pore ordering as a state-of-the-art foundation to advance the conversion of CO to formic acid. In this manner, slurries are cast onto polymeric carrier 2 film under a precision gap, where the slurry subsequently undergoes a rapid temperature transition that facilitates the growth of ice crystals from the bed to the surface of the tape. As the ice crystals nucleate and grow, the suspended particulate is excluded, generating graded, acicular ice crystals that can be sublimed under a vacuum to form the pores (Figure 1). Optimized freeze tape casting can be achieved on slurries as thin as 100 microns and up to and beyond 1 cm, providing opportunities to functionalize the freeze tape cast layers for device consolidation and far exceeds the classic range of traditional tape casting. The proposed innovation in materials processing is based on developments in freeze tape-casting. The guiding data for the lateral grading concept is based on the change in pore volume, as shown in Figure 2. At constant temperature, hence the solidification rate, as the solids loading of particulate content of the slurry is decreased, the porosity 12 is shown to increase in a nearly linear fashion. The increased porosity (overall pore volume) is realized through both an increase in pore size and pore density of the cast structure. Recent activities at MSU have shown the capability to freeze tape cast as low as 10 vol% solids loading, yielding approximately 90% porosity. The upper bound on solids is near 45 vol% solids loading, above which particle rejection during solidification is halted from particle crowding. This provides a basis for tailoring total porosity in freeze tape cast membranes from ~ 50 – 90%. Importantly, the low solids loading utilized for fabricating porous bodies is highly conducive to environmentally friendly water-based aqueous processing that combines large areas and thin cross sections for substrate materials in which porous materials are often sought (Sofie, S.
